Title: Encoding of speech sounds at auditory brainstem level in good and poor hearing aid performers.

Journal/Date: Brazilian journal of otorhinolaryngology (2017)

MeSH Keywords: Acoustic Stimulation, Adaptation, Physiological, Adolescent, Adult, Aged, Auditory Threshold, Evoked Potentials, Auditory, Brain Stem, Female


--- ABSTRACT ---
[INTRODUCTION]: Hearing aids are prescribed to alleviate loss of audibility. It has been reported that about 31% of hearing aid users reject their own hearing aid because of annoyance towards background noise. The reason for dissatisfaction can be located anywhere from the hearing aid microphone till the integrity of neurons along the auditory pathway.
[OBJECTIVES]: To measure spectra from the output of hearing aid at the ear canal level and frequency following response recorded at the auditory brainstem from individuals with hearing impairment.
[METHODS]: A total of sixty participants having moderate sensorineural hearing impairment with age range from 15 to 65 years were involved. Each participant was classified as either Good or Poor Hearing aid Performers based on acceptable noise level measure. Stimuli /da/ and /si/ were presented through loudspeaker at 65dB SPL. At the ear canal, the spectra were measured in the unaided and aided conditions. At auditory brainstem, frequency following response were recorded to the same stimuli from the participants.
[RESULTS]: Spectrum measured in each condition at ear canal was same in good hearing aid performers and poor hearing aid performers. At brainstem level, better F0 encoding; F0 and F1 energies were significantly higher in good hearing aid performers than in poor hearing aid performers. Though the hearing aid spectra were almost same between good hearing aid performers and poor hearing aid performers, subtle physiological variations exist at the auditory brainstem.
[CONCLUSION]: The result of the present study suggests that neural encoding of speech sound at the brainstem level might be mediated distinctly in good hearing aid performers from that of poor hearing aid performers. Thus, it can be inferred that subtle physiological changes are evident at the auditory brainstem in a person who is willing to accept noise from those who are not willing to accept noise.

[OBJECTIVE]: Individuals with age-related hearing loss (ARHL) can restore some loss of the auditory function with the use of hearing aids (HAs). However, what remains unknown are the physiological mechanisms that underlie how the brain changes with exposure to amplified sounds though the use of HAs. We aimed to examine behavioral and physiological changes induced by HAs.
[METHODS]: Thirty-five older-adults with moderate ARHL with no history of hearing aid use were fit with HAs tested in aided and unaided conditions, and divided into experimental and control groups. The experimental group used HAs during a period of six months. The control group did not use HAs during this period, but were given the opportunity to use them after the completion of the study. Both groups underwent testing protocols six months apart. Outcome measures included behavioral (speech-in-noise measures, self-assessment questionnaires) and electrophysiological brainstem recordings (frequency-following responses) to the speech syllable /ga/ in two quiet conditions and in six-talker babble noise.
[RESULTS]: The experimental group reported subjective benefits on self-assessment questionnaires. Significant physiological changes were observed in the experimental group, specifically a reduction in fundamental frequency magnitude, while no change was observed in controls, yielding a significant time × group interaction. Furthermore, peak latencies remained stable in the experimental group but were significantly delayed in the control group after six months. Significant correlations between behavioral and physiological changes were also observed.
[CONCLUSIONS]: The findings suggest that HAs may alter subcortical processing and offset neural timing delay; however, further investigation is needed to understand cortical changes and HA effects on cognitive processing.

Electroencephalography could serve as an objective tool to evaluate hearing aid benefit in infants who are developmentally unable to participate in hearing tests. We investigated whether speech-evoked envelope following responses (EFRs), a type of electroencephalography-based measure, could predict improved audibility with the use of a hearing aid in children with mild-to-severe permanent, mainly sensorineural, hearing loss. In 18 children, EFRs were elicited by six male-spoken band-limited phonemic stimuli--the first formants of /u/ and /i/, the second and higher formants of /u/ and /i/, and the fricatives /s/ and /∫/--presented together as /su∫i/. EFRs were recorded between the vertex and nape, when /su∫i/ was presented at 55, 65, and 75 dB SPL using insert earphones in unaided conditions and individually fit hearing aids in aided conditions. EFR amplitude and detectability improved with the use of a hearing aid, and the degree of improvement in EFR amplitude was dependent on the extent of change in behavioral thresholds between unaided and aided conditions. EFR detectability was primarily influenced by audibility; higher sensation level stimuli had an increased probability of detection. Overall EFR sensitivity in predicting audibility was significantly higher in aided (82.1%) than unaided conditions (66.5%) and did not vary as a function of stimulus or frequency. EFR specificity in ascertaining inaudibility was 90.8%. Aided improvement in EFR detectability was a significant predictor of hearing aid-facilitated change in speech discrimination accuracy. Results suggest that speech-evoked EFRs could be a useful objective tool in predicting hearing aid benefit in children with hearing loss.

Title: Effect of digital noise reduction processing on subcortical speech encoding and relationship to behavioral outcomes.

Journal/Date: Scientific reports (2025)

MeSH Keywords: Humans, Speech Perception, Male, Noise, Female, Adult, Young Adult, Speech


--- ABSTRACT ---
Perceptual benefits from digital noise reduction (NR) vary among individuals with different noise tolerance and sensitivity to distortions introduced in NR-processed speech; however, the physiological bases of the variance are understudied. Here, we developed objective measures of speech encoding in the ascending pathway as candidate measures of individual noise tolerance and sensitivity to NR-processed speech using the brainstem responses to speech syllable /da/. The speech-evoked brainstem response was found to be sensitive to the addition of noise and NR processing. The NR effects on the consonant and vowel portion of the responses were robustly quantified using response-to-response correlation metrics and spectral amplitude ratios, respectively. Further, the f0 amplitude ratios between conditions correlated with behavioral accuracy with NR. These findings suggest that investigating the NR effects on bottom-up speech encoding using brainstem measures is feasible and that individual subcortical encoding of NR-processed speech may relate to individual behavioral outcomes with NR.

key_findings.finding: The clearest direct human comparison is a 2017 study of 60 participants aged 15–65 years with moderate sensorineural hearing loss. Participants were classified as good versus poor hearing-aid performers using the Acceptable Noise Level (ANL) measure. With /da/ and /si/ presented at 65 dB SPL, hearing-aid output spectra at the ear canal were similar between groups, but speech-evoked FFRs showed significantly better fundamental-frequency (F0) encoding and significantly greater F0 and F1 spectral energy in good performers. This supports a group difference in subcortical speech encoding, in the direction of stronger low-frequency/formant representation in good performers.

key_findings.finding: A 2018 longitudinal human study examined 35 older adults with moderate age-related hearing loss who were new hearing-aid users versus a no-use control group, rather than pre-defined good versus poor performers. After 6 months, hearing-aid use altered speech-evoked FFRs to /ga/ in quiet and six-talker babble: F0 magnitude decreased, peak latencies remained stable, whereas controls showed delayed peak latencies. Physiological changes correlated with behavioral changes. This supports hearing-aid-use-related subcortical plasticity, but it does not directly establish a baseline good-versus-poor performer difference.

source_tools.relevance: Human longitudinal FFR evidence relevant to hearing-aid use, with explicit limitation that groups were use versus no-use rather than outcome strata

key_findings.finding: In 18 children with mild-to-severe permanent, mainly sensorineural hearing loss, speech-evoked envelope-following responses improved in individually fitted aided versus unaided conditions. Aided EFR detectability and amplitude reflected improved audibility, and aided improvement in EFR detectability significantly predicted hearing-aid-facilitated change in speech-discrimination accuracy. This is predictive/aided-versus-unaided evidence, not a direct comparison of independently defined good and poor hearing-aid outcome groups.

source_tools.relevance: Direct human speech-envelope/EFR study with pediatric population and outcome-prediction result

key_findings.finding: A 2025 human study of 26 adults tested speech-evoked brainstem responses to /da/ in quiet, noise, and digital-noise-reduction conditions. Brainstem response similarity and spectral measures were sensitive to noise-reduction processing, and f0 amplitude ratios correlated with behavioral accuracy under noise reduction. However, the study did not compare predefined good versus poor hearing-aid users; it provides mechanistic support that individual subcortical speech encoding relates to behavioral benefit from processing.

source_tools.relevance: Human subcortical speech-in-noise/processing evidence and explicit behavioral correlation, but not a good-versus-poor HA outcome comparison

key_findings.finding: Overall, the available evidence supports a likely group difference in auditory-brainstem speech encoding between good and poor hearing-aid performers, based primarily on one direct FFR comparison. Evidence for envelope tracking/EFR and subcortical speech-in-noise measures is supportive but indirect because most studies compare aided versus unaided states, hearing-aid use versus nonuse, or continuous behavioral performance rather than prespecified good/poor outcome groups. The literature is therefore suggestive rather than extensive or definitive.

source_tools.relevance: Synthesis grounded in the direct comparison and complementary indirect studies

entities.name: PMID:27516129
observations: In 60 participants aged 15–65 years with moderate sensorineural hearing loss, good hearing-aid performers defined by Acceptable Noise Level showed stronger speech-evoked FFR F0 encoding and greater F0/F1 spectral energy than poor performers for /da/ and /si/ at 65 dB SPL; hearing-aid output spectra were similar at the ear canal.

entities.name: PMID:29677689
observations: In 35 older adults with moderate age-related hearing loss, six months of hearing-aid use altered speech-evoked FFRs to /ga/ in quiet and babble; physiological changes correlated with behavioral changes, but participants were not preclassified as good or poor performers.

source_tools.relevance: Indirect evidence for hearing-aid-related subcortical plasticity
